newsitem.title: USA: California suicide cult wanted to make a movie.
newsitem.headline: California suicide cult wanted to make a movie.

text.p: Members of the Heaven's Gate cult had been trying to make a movie in the months before their mass suicide in California in a bid to spread their bizarre views across America, according to two film producers.

Alex Papas, a Phoenix producer who met the group when they were living in Arizona, said they used him in late 1995 to launch the project, which was based on their beliefs about life on Earth and moving on to the "Kingdom of God."
The NBC network had shown some interest in producing a movie before deciding against it.

Rick Singer, a Los Angeles television and movie producer and Papas' partner, said on Saturday he got a call from one of the cult members only two weeks ago and was stunned when he learned of their mass suicide.
"I was shocked," he said. "They were a little weird the way they looked and dressed, but they were so eager and so enthusiastic.
"It would have been more likely that they would have wanted to live for a couple of hundred years just so they could keep their eyes glued to a telescope," he added.
Papas, who runs Way Out Pictures, said he met two cult members in September 1995 when they subleased a $450,000 home in Paradise Valley, Ariz., an affluent Phoenix suburb.
The group paid $3,400 a month to rent the 5,400-square-foot, six-bedroom house. The lease was signed by Margaret Richter, 46, of California, and Susan Paup, of New Mexico.
Within weeks, Papas said the group gave him a 223-page screenplay after learning he was a movie producer.

Entitled "Beyond Human: Return of the Next Level," it featured motherships, alien abductions and clashes between bad reptile-like aliens and benevolent ones for control of the Earth. It told of the ability to rise up to a level several flights above humans.

Members worked to refine the rambling science-fiction script in hopes of getting it on television. The project was actively discussed just two weeks before the 39 members committed suicide in Rancho Sante Fe.

"They were rational, lucid, reasonable people," said Papas, who said 15 group members lived in Arizona until last June. "They were easy to talk to and were real interested in getting their script out into the public."

Papas said he worked for months with group members who identified themselves as Otis Paceman and Rio DiAngelo, before turning the project over to Singer. DiAngelo is believed to be the member chosen to remain alive to promote the cult's views and who made the call to alert authorities about the suicides.
Singer said he presented a revised script to NBC and that the network was initially interested before deciding against it.
He said he had several lunches with cult members after that and then got a call two weeks ago from DiAngelo.
"He said he had left the group and he wanted to move forward with the teleplay," Singer said. "That's what we were planning to do when all this happened."
Singer said he could not have imagined that the Heaven's Gate members he knew could have killed themselves.
"They were so thankful about what I was doing." Singer said he learned of the mass suicide when a friend called him and told him to turn on the television.
"I was shocked," he said. "I would have given long odds that they would have wanted to do something like this.
